claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by oxidation-induced segregation of Ti, Al, and Cr at grain boundaries.
Oxidizing exposure forms and grows brittle oxide-based precipitates along grain boundaries.
At temperatures starting around 950 K, sigma-like phases can grow and preferentially locate at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary sigma-like precipitation can significantly reduce mechanical and chemical properties.
Boundary precipitates reduce intergranular cohesion and act as weak links.
Accelerated grain-boundary diffusion promotes oxidation of Ti, Al, and Cr during high-temperature oxidizing exposure.
Oxide or sigma-like boundary precipitates coalesce, create stress concentrations, and trigger intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure.
Suppressing oxygen under reducing conditions delays oxidation-induced boundary embrittlement.
Reducing conditions may promote alternative in-situ phase transformations arising from non-equilibrium segregation that weaken the alloy.
The as-manufactured material is a single-phase FCC alloy with relatively homogeneous elemental distribution.
The as-manufactured material contains fine, possibly supersaturated precipitates or limited initial precipitation.
Phase transformations and oxidation kinetics relevant to degradation are active over approximately 950–1100 K.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a higher density of brittle grain-boundary precipitates than either the starting state or reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will cause pronounced reductions in hardness and intergranular fracture toughness and earlier crack initiation.
Reducing exposure will yield fewer grain-boundary precipitates and delayed or altered failure modes relative to oxidizing exposure.
Degradation kinetics and the failure threshold are sensitive to composition nuances and additive-manufacturing history.

contradictions.description: The material is described as single-phase FCC while also being described as containing fine or limited initial precipitates. Unless those features are compositionally identical FCC domains, precipitates imply an additional phase and conflict with the single-phase characterization.
